the formulation of constitutitive equations for the mechanical behavior of living soft tissues, which exhibit a marked increase in stiffness with increasing strain, or, more precisely, with the development of constitutive equations which describe the mechanical behavior of soft tissues in which the stiffness is a function of the strain.
the formulation of constitutives equations that describe the mechanical behavior of soft living tissues and include as special cases the classical theory of linearly elastic solids
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the theory of large elastic deformation of a continuum has been extended to include the effect of a threshold strain, below which the material is assumed to behave as a linearly elastic solid, and above which the material is characterized by a stress-strain relationship that is nonlinear.
the theory presented in this paper provides an excellent mathematical framework for describing the behavior of living soft tissues.

the constitutive equations of the type presented in this report are capable of describing the mechanical behavior of soft living tissues and that these equations are unique in the sense that they assure uniqueness of solution of a broad class of problems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how to formulate constitutive equations for a broad class (but not all) of soft living tissues that describe their mechanical behavior.
we developed the first constitutive model of living soft tissue that is based on a fundamental physical principle and can be derived from first principles.
we have developed a constitutive model for soft tissues which is able to capture their mechanical response to a wide range of loading conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the theory of nonlinear viscoelasticity is not limited to the case of small deformations.

the mechanical response of living soft tissues, such as the heart and the brain, can be described by a constitutive equation that has two parts: one that is linear in the strain (Hookean) and the other that is nonlinear in the strain.

the constitutive equations for soft biological materials can be formulated in terms of the strain energy density function, as in classical elasticity, and that the constitutive equation for a material with a yield stress can be obtained as the limit of a constitutive equation with a smooth strain energy function as the yield stress goes to zero.
